title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can serve as an effective tool for automated writing evaluation (AWE) in higher education English-as-a-new-language (ENL) instruction, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback over feedback from a human tutor. The motivation is practical and pedagogical: as large language models such as GPT-4 become more accessible, educators need evidence on whether they can support writing instruction without harming learning outcomes.

The article reports two studies conducted at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region during Spring 2023. In Study 1, 48 ENL university students were placed into a control group receiving feedback from a trained human tutor or an experimental group receiving GPT-4-generated feedback over a six-week repeated-measures quasi-experimental design. Writing quality was assessed with pre- and posttests using an analytic rubric. In Study 2, a separate group of 43 ENL students received both AI and human feedback on weekly assignments and completed preference surveys plus open-ended responses.

Study 1 found no significant difference in writing gains between students who received AI-generated feedback and those who received human tutor feedback. Both groups improved similarly over time, suggesting that GPT-4-based feedback was not inferior to human feedback in this context, but also did not produce superior gains. Study 2 showed a near-even split in student preference between AI and human feedback. Students who preferred AI emphasized clarity, specificity, and availability, while those favoring human feedback valued interaction, engagement, and opportunities for follow-up. The authors conclude that a blended model combining AI-generated feedback with human tutoring may be the most beneficial approach.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based chatbot/LLM interface used to generate text feedback on student writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4 within ChatGPT to generate corrective feedback on ENL students' weekly writing assignments and to compare AI-generated feedback with human tutor feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48 ENL university students; analytic sample n=48 minus 1 posttest-only student), AI-generated feedback from GPT-4 did not produce superior writing gains relative to human tutor feedback. Both groups improved similarly over six weeks, and the group-by-time interaction was not statistically significant, F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063.
findings.measure: Pretest-posttest writing scores on an analytic rubric assessing content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43 ENL students; weekly survey responses varied from 32 to 41, average 37.7), student preference for GPT-4 feedback was nearly evenly split with preference for human tutor feedback. Grand means were very close across satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference, with slightly higher means for human tutor feedback on each paired item.
findings.measure: Weekly student preference survey on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall feedback preference

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single quasi-experimental study plus a survey/mixed-methods study, not a randomized trial or meta-analysis. The design is direct but has moderate methodological limitations, so the evidence is informative but not high-certainty.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports no statistically significant improvement in writing outcomes from AI-generated feedback over human tutor feedback, with a small interaction effect (partial eta squared=0.063). Student preference is mixed/even, suggesting unclear practical impact overall.
